newsitem.title: UK: UK to review company law after Saunders ruling.
newsitem.headline: UK to review company law after Saunders ruling.

text.p: UK's Department of Trade and Industry is studying a judgement by the European Court of Human Rights in favour of former Guinness Plc chairman Ernest Saunders to see whether it will require a change in British law.
"All options will be considered including the possibility of legislative change and we will make an announcement as soon as possible," said a DTI spokeswoman on Tuesday.

Under the UK's 1985 Companies Act DTI Inspectors can require suspects to answer their questions under threat of imprisonment. The powers extend to the Serious Fraud Office as well as DTI inspectors and some liquidators.

The European Convention on Human Rights, which Britain has signed, protects individuals from being obliged to incriminate themselves and Saunders claimed he was deprived of a fair hearing as safeguarded by Article 5 of the Convention.

The DTI has 340 cases going through the UK courts where some of the evidence obtained has been gained through the use of its compulsion powers. But the vast majority of these cases relate to company insolvency rather than insider dealing.

"There is public concern over the woefully inadaquate handling of a number of high profile City cases by the Serious Fraud Office and the DTI," said Treasury opposition Labour party spokesman Nichael O'Brien in an interview.

"This ruling raises new questions about whether DTI inspectors can use their powers under the legislation to tackle City problems in the future and whether the present legislation is adequate," he added.
